taxonomyNote: Formerly treated as one species ('Short-horned Lizard') with P. hernandesi; Montana Field Guide and NatureServe treat them as separate species. WDFW lists the family as Iguanidae; NatureServe uses Phrynosomatidae.
fieldMarks: Toad-shaped: blunt snout, squat flattened body, short legs and a short triangular tail.
Spines project from the back of the head, with fringe-like spines along the sides.
Back is mottled white, gray, beige, tan, brown or black, sometimes yellow or orange, with dark blotches in transverse rows; underside white, sometimes with a yellow or gray wash.
Small: about 2.5 inches (without tail) as an adult; females larger than males; males have enlarged femoral pores.
Head horns are small and project nearly vertically, and lack the wide notch that gives the greater short-horned lizard a heart-shaped head (Montana Field Guide).
behavior: Live-bearing; gives birth to 3-15 young, mainly August to mid-September.
Surface active roughly March-early November in Washington; mid-day active in spring and fall, inactive at mid-day in summer.
Diet is primarily ants (about three-quarters in adults) plus other insects; newborns feed almost exclusively on ants.
Colour tracks the substrate, which makes it cryptic; burrows into soil or uses rodent burrows when inactive.
habitat: Semiarid plains to high mountains in open, sparsely vegetated shrubby or openly wooded areas: sagebrush, bunchgrass, pinyon-juniper, open pine.
Soil varies from rocky to sandy; in Washington occupies shrubsteppe.
range: Eastern Washington south to northeastern California and east to northern Nevada and eastern Idaho; an old record exists from extreme southwestern Montana. Historical records near Osoyoos Lake, British Columbia, but considered extirpated from Canada.

lookalikes.name: Greater short-horned lizard
lookalikes.howToTell: Larger; wide notch between the head horns gives a heart-shaped head, horns project horizontally.
